questions.stem: All items in a batch tend to be heavy or light together. What is questionable about sqrt(n) times individual SD for the total?
questions.explanation: Positive dependence can make total variation larger than the independent formula predicts.

questions.stem: For a normal model, where is the 10th percentile?
questions.explanation: The lowest tenth ends on the lower side of the symmetric center.

questions.stem: A sample's mean file size is 18 KB. The study aims to estimate the mean across all files on a server. What does 18 KB represent?
questions.explanation: A sample mean summarizes its observed files and estimates a population mean.

source.slide_title: The terms in a mean study

choices: The exact population mean regardless of selection.
The size of every file on the server.
An estimate based on the sampled files.

questions.stem: How does no arrivals in the next 5 minutes relate to waiting more than 5 minutes for the next arrival?
questions.explanation: No event before the cutoff means the next event occurs after it.
choices: They describe the same event, ignoring a zero-probability boundary.
The first requires exactly one arrival.

questions.stem: A supervisor predicts the expected total number of jobs across many sessions. What does that prediction describe?
questions.explanation: Expected totals describe long-run averages, even when actual totals vary.
choices: The exact total in the next batch.
The average total across repeated batches of sessions.
The most jobs any batch could contain.
The most likely total in every possible model.

questions.stem: A sample has 2 successes and 98 failures. Does a large total alone justify the ordinary normal-approximation proportion interval?
questions.explanation: The success-failure check concerns both counts, not just total n.
choices: No; the observed success count is too sparse.
No; proportions cannot be estimated at all.

questions.stem: Two successes in four trials can occur in several orders. Why must all those orders be considered?
questions.explanation: A count aggregates several distinct trial sequences.
choices: The count event includes every order with two successes.
The expected count is an order.
Only the first successful order can occur.
Different orders are the same elementary outcome.

questions.stem: A bell-shaped distribution has mean 20 and SD 2. Approximately which interval contains 95%?
questions.explanation: The empirical rule uses about two standard deviations on each side for a bell-shaped distribution.

questions.stem: P(A)=0.2 but P(A AND B)=0.3. Why is this impossible?
questions.explanation: The intersection is a subset of A and cannot be more probable than A.
choices: The overlap must always equal zero.
The overlap cannot exceed the probability of A.

questions.stem: A mean interval is 10 to 14. How should a proposed mean of 12 be described?
questions.explanation: Every interior value is compatible with the interval; the midpoint is not a certainty.
choices: Proved to be the exact population mean.
Compatible with the interval, without being proved exact.

figure.alt: Interval 10 to 14 and proposed mean 12 marked at the center.

data.alt: Interval 10 to 14 and proposed mean 12 marked at the center.

questions.stem: Data are 0, 8, 9, 9, 10. Which center is lower?
questions.explanation: The isolated low value pulls the mean below the median of 9.

questions.stem: The slides recommend plus-four when confidence is at least 90% and n>=10. Does n=24 at 85% confidence meet that recommendation?
questions.explanation: Both stated recommendations must be met; this is distinct from the ordinary interval count check.
choices: No; the confidence level is below the stated threshold.
Yes; plus-four has no stated conditions.

questions.stem: 20 students use both devices; 40 use tablets and 80 use laptops. Which conditional probability is larger?
questions.explanation: The fractions are 20/40 versus 20/80, with different conditioning denominators.
choices: Neither can use the overlap count.

questions.stem: A symmetric 90% confidence construction leaves what fraction in each tail?
questions.explanation: The excluded 10% splits equally across two tails.

questions.stem: A payout variable is measured in dollars. What units belong to its variance?
questions.explanation: Variance uses squared deviations from the expected payout.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: A sample grows from 50 to 51 observations. Must its mean move closer to the population mean?
questions.explanation: Long-run stabilization does not guarantee improvement at each additional observation.
choices: Yes; every increase improves the estimate.
No; larger samples always worsen estimates.
Yes; the law of large numbers guarantees monotone improvement.
No; individual additions can move it either way.

questions.stem: A roster repeats a ten-person pattern, with every tenth entry a team leader. Why could taking every tenth entry be problematic?
questions.explanation: Periodicity in the list can produce a systematically unrepresentative sample.
choices: A larger interval always makes selection random.
The sampling interval can align with the repeating pattern.

questions.skill_group: Continuous densities, areas, and cumulative probabilities
questions.stem: A continuous model gives F(6)=0.70. What does that say?
questions.explanation: The cumulative function gives probability up through the cutoff.
choices: 70% of modeled durations are at most 6.

questions.stem: P(X>50)=0.50 and P(X>60)=0.10. Given X>50, what is P(X>60)?
questions.explanation: The smaller upper-tail event is contained in the conditioned event, giving 0.10/0.50.

questions.stem: A sample is drawn without replacement from a box containing marked and unmarked cards. When must the sample contain a marked card?
questions.explanation: There are too few unmarked cards to fill a sample larger than their number.
choices: Only if every card in the box is marked.
Whenever the sample size is less than the number of unmarked cards.
Whenever one marked card is present in the box.
When the sample size exceeds the number of unmarked cards.

questions.stem: For known population SD and fixed confidence, n quadruples. What happens to the margin of error?
questions.explanation: The mean interval margin scales with 1/sqrt(n).

questions.skill_group: Continuous densities, areas, and cumulative probabilities
questions.stem: An exact continuous duration has P(X=4)=0. Can a timer report 4 seconds?
questions.explanation: A rounded recorded value can have positive probability even though an exact point has zero area.
choices: No; 4 seconds can never be recorded.
Yes; rounding collects a positive-width interval of exact values.
Only if the density equals zero everywhere.
Only if the model becomes discrete before rounding.

questions.stem: 40 students use laptops, 25 use tablets, and 10 use both. Why subtract 10 when counting either device?
questions.explanation: Subtracting one copy of the overlap counts each person once.
choices: Both-device users must be excluded entirely.
The overlap does not use either device.
Adding the first two counts includes the overlap twice.
Subtraction is required because the sample is random.

figure.alt: Venn regions: 30 laptop only, 10 both, 15 tablet only. The illustrated universe is the 55 users of either device.

data.alt: Venn regions: 30 laptop only, 10 both, 15 tablet only. The illustrated universe is the 55 users of either device.

questions.stem: A basic box plot reports minimum 0, Q1=2, median 3, Q3=4, maximum 20. Which comparison is supported?
questions.explanation: Using the displayed summary, the upper segment spans 20-4=16 units and the lower segment spans 2-0=2 units. Segment length describes numerical spread, not an exact observation count; quartile conventions and ties can affect those counts.
choices: The segment from Q3 to the maximum spans a wider numerical range than the segment from the minimum to Q1.
The plot establishes the exact mean.
The upper segment must contain three times as many observations.
The lower segment contains no observations.

figure.alt: Basic box plot: minimum 0, Q1 2, median 3, Q3 4, maximum 20. Whiskers show min and max.

data.alt: Basic box plot: minimum 0, Q1 2, median 3, Q3 4, maximum 20. Whiskers show min and max.

questions.stem: A teacher draws cards without replacement until the first marked card. Why is the draw number generally neither binomial nor geometric?
questions.explanation: The stopping rule rules out binomial counting, and the changing pool violates the geometric assumptions.
choices: The trial count is not fixed, and the chance can change between draws.
Stopping at the first success always makes the count binomial.
A success has to be a desirable outcome.

questions.stem: Why represent a single binomial count by an interval when using a normal approximation?
questions.explanation: The interval lets continuous area approximate the discrete probability mass.
choices: An interval has area under a continuous curve, while a single point has zero area.
The normal distribution has positive probability at every exact point.
The count can take fractional values.
A count always equals its expected value.

questions.stem: A distribution has equal peaks near 2 and 8 and is symmetric around 5. What follows?
questions.explanation: A symmetric distribution can be bimodal with its center between peaks.
choices: Symmetry does not require a single peak.

questions.stem: Two normal curves share SD but have different means. What is equal?
questions.explanation: A common SD gives identical shape and width; different means shift the curves.
choices: Their probabilities below every fixed cutoff.

questions.stem: Three reported percentages are 33.3%, 33.3%, and 33.3%. What most reasonably explains the 99.9% total?
questions.explanation: Rounding can make displayed percentages differ slightly from 100%.

questions.stem: A value equals its distribution's mean. What is its z-score?
questions.explanation: Its deviation from the mean is zero.

questions.stem: Mean is 30 and SD is 4. Which value has z=1.5?
questions.explanation: Add 1.5 times 4 to the mean.

questions.stem: A box plot has median 6. Can it reveal exactly how many observations equal 5?
questions.explanation: A box plot compresses the data into a few summary positions.
choices: No; the summary does not retain those exact counts.

questions.stem: All items in a batch tend to be heavy or light together. What is questionable about sqrt(n) times individual SD for the total?
questions.explanation: Positive dependence can make total variation larger than the independent formula predicts.

questions.stem: An exponential density extends far right with diminishing height. What does that say about very long waits?
questions.explanation: An unbounded right tail allows large values without making them frequent.
choices: They must occur as often as short waits.
They are possible but less common than short waits.
They are impossible once the mean is exceeded.

questions.stem: Everyone in a few selected clubs is surveyed. What challenges treating all responses as independent?
questions.explanation: Cluster membership can introduce within-group dependence.
choices: The sample proportion cannot be computed.
Club members cannot have binary responses.
Randomly selecting clubs guarantees individual independence.
Members of the same club may have correlated responses.

questions.stem: Campus A has 30 users among 60 students; campus B has 40 among 100. Which has the higher use rate?
questions.explanation: The rates are 50% and 40%; denominators matter.
choices: Counts alone prove campus B has the higher rate.

questions.stem: A one-sample t interval uses n=16. What degrees of freedom are used?
questions.explanation: A one-sample mean t method uses n-1 degrees of freedom.

questions.stem: A researcher stops after a fixed number of draws and counts marked tokens. Which detail best distinguishes the binomial and hypergeometric settings?
questions.explanation: The two models use different sampling designs even though both count successes in a fixed number of draws.
choices: Whether the recorded result is a whole number.
Whether marked is a desirable outcome.
Whether a fixed number of draws is used.
Whether each token is returned and the pool remixed before the next draw.

questions.stem: The sample is an unordered set of cables. Why count combinations rather than different orders of the same set?
questions.explanation: Unordered sampling treats permutations of the same selected set as one sample.
choices: Every sample set has only one cable.
Reordering the same selected cables does not create a new sample set.
Selection order determines whether a cable is faulty.

questions.stem: A discrete probability table has a row at the cutoff. How do the events below the cutoff and at or below the cutoff differ?
questions.explanation: The words at or below include equality.
choices: Both exclude the row at the cutoff.
Only the second includes the row at the cutoff.
They include opposite sides of the cutoff.
Only the first includes the row at the cutoff.

questions.stem: Daily print totals are shown in a histogram instead of a time-series graph. What information is lost?
questions.explanation: A histogram summarizes the distribution without retaining chronology.
choices: Which total occurred on which date.

questions.stem: The plus-four estimate adds two successes and two failures. With 8 successes out of 40, what adjusted fraction is used?
questions.explanation: The adjusted count is x+2 and the adjusted total is n+4.

questions.stem: Why is adding signed deviations from the sample mean unsuitable as a spread measure?
questions.explanation: Signed deviations sum to zero even when observations are widely spread.
choices: The mean is always the largest value.
It necessarily counts each value twice.

questions.stem: A researcher stops after a fixed number of draws and counts marked tokens. Which detail best distinguishes the binomial and hypergeometric settings?
questions.explanation: The two models use different sampling designs even though both count successes in a fixed number of draws.
choices: Whether the recorded result is a whole number.
Whether marked is a desirable outcome.
Whether each token is returned and the pool remixed before the next draw.
Whether a fixed number of draws is used.

questions.stem: The course uses N(mean, SD). A technician expects readings from N(40,6) to cluster near 6. What is the best correction?
questions.explanation: The first parameter is the center; the SD measures variation around it, rather than another center.
choices: They cluster near 6; 40 is the sample size.
The readings cluster near 40; 6 describes their spread.
The model allows only the two values 6 and 40.

questions.stem: Mean is 100, SD is 10, and the supplied 90th-percentile z is 1.28. What is the corresponding value?
questions.explanation: Return to original units with mean plus z times SD.

questions.stem: Four jobs have a mean of 5 pages. What is the total number of pages?
questions.explanation: Total equals number of observations times their mean.

questions.stem: To find the probability of A followed by B when the stages may be dependent, which expression fits?
questions.explanation: The general multiplication rule uses the appropriate conditional probability.
choices: P(A) times P(B) without checking independence.

questions.stem: A supplied normal distribution of sample means gives cumulative probabilities 0.15 at 8 and 0.85 at 12. What is the probability between 8 and 12?
questions.explanation: Subtract cumulative areas at the endpoints.

questions.stem: Both endpoints of a uniform model increase by 4. What happens to its mean and SD?
questions.explanation: A translation shifts location but preserves distances.
choices: SD rises by 4; mean stays unchanged.
Mean rises by 4; SD stays unchanged.

questions.stem: A random sample of 80 enrolled students reports 30% support for later hours. Which conclusion is justified?
questions.explanation: A sample result is evidence about a population, not an exact census result.
choices: Exactly 24 students in the entire college support later hours.
Exactly 30% of all students support later hours.
30% describes the sample and estimates population support.

questions.stem: A recorded file size is far above the rest. What should happen before deleting it?
questions.explanation: An unusual value can be valid and informative; deletion needs a defensible reason.
choices: Check whether it is an error or a genuine unusual file.
Keep it only if the mean equals the median.
Delete it because all outliers are mistakes.

questions.stem: One hundred valid 95% intervals are constructed in repeated sampling. Must exactly 95 cover the mean?
questions.explanation: A long-run proportion is not an exact finite-sample quota.
choices: No; the coverage count itself can vary.
Yes; any other count proves bias.
Yes; the confidence level fixes that count.

questions.stem: Arrival rates sharply rise at lunchtime. What is questionable about a single exponential waiting model over the whole day?
questions.explanation: A single exponential waiting model of this kind assumes a stable arrival rate.
choices: A constant rate across the whole period.

questions.stem: Normal models have the same mean. For a fixed cutoff below that mean, which has the larger lower-tail probability?
questions.explanation: A wider curve places more area beyond a fixed cutoff away from its center.
choices: The model with the larger SD.
The one with more recorded observations regardless of SD.
The model with the smaller SD.

questions.stem: Population SD is 12 and n=36, with independent observations. sqrt(36)=6. What is the mean's SE?
questions.explanation: Divide population SD by the supplied square root of sample size.

questions.stem: The numbers of pages in six jobs are 1, 2, 2, 4, 4, 5. Which statement about the mode is correct?
questions.explanation: The values 2 and 4 each occur twice, more often than any other value.
choices: The mode is 3, halfway between 2 and 4.

questions.stem: A small prize is common and a large prize is rare. Why is the midpoint between the prizes generally a poor estimate of the expected payout?
questions.explanation: Expected value weights each outcome by its probability.
choices: It gives the two prizes equal weight despite their different chances.
The expected payout must equal the larger prize.
Only the larger prize determines the mean.
The small prize does not count toward the average.

questions.stem: For a standard normal variable, compare P(Z<-1.4) and P(Z>1.4).
questions.explanation: Normal symmetry makes opposite equal-distance tails equal.

questions.stem: Two mutually exclusive events each have positive probability. Can they be independent?
questions.explanation: For positive-probability disjoint events, the intersection is zero but the product is positive.
choices: No; one occurring makes the other impossible.
Only if their probabilities add to 1.

questions.stem: A count variable has expected value 0.4. What does that mean?
questions.explanation: An expectation is an average, not necessarily a possible individual value.
choices: Exactly 40% of sessions must contain one event.
Its long-run average can be 0.4 despite integer observations.
A single session must contain 0.4 events.

questions.stem: On a die, A is even and B is greater than 3. Which results satisfy at least one condition?
questions.explanation: The union includes all outcomes in either event, counting overlaps once.

questions.stem: Remove 100 from 1, 2, 3, 4, 100. What happens to the mean and median?
questions.explanation: The mean changes from 22 to 2.5; the median changes from 3 to 2.5.
choices: Both decrease, with a much larger decrease in the mean.
The mean increases and median decreases.
The median increases and mean stays unchanged.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: All individual waits lie between 2 and 14. A normal approximation gives a tiny chance that a mean is below 2. How should this be interpreted?
questions.explanation: An average cannot fall below the minimum possible individual value.
choices: The true sample mean can actually be below every observation.
The observations must include negative waits.
It is approximation error outside the true support.
The normal model is exact at every tail.

questions.stem: A narrow interval uses only the fastest successful jobs to estimate the mean for all jobs. What is its main limitation?
questions.explanation: Precision cannot repair systematically excluded outcomes.
choices: Adding decimal places removes selection bias.
Biased selection can make the interval misleading despite narrow width.

questions.stem: Two successes in four trials can occur in several orders. Why must all those orders be considered?
questions.explanation: A count aggregates several distinct trial sequences.
choices: Different orders are the same elementary outcome.
Only the first successful order can occur.
The count event includes every order with two successes.
The expected count is an order.

questions.stem: Arrival rates sharply rise at lunchtime. What is questionable about a single exponential waiting model over the whole day?
questions.explanation: A single exponential waiting model of this kind assumes a stable arrival rate.
choices: A constant rate across the whole period.

questions.stem: A symmetric interval is 8 to 12. What is the margin of error?
questions.explanation: Margin of error is half the total width.

questions.stem: Campus A has 30 users among 60 students; campus B has 40 among 100. Which has the higher use rate?
questions.explanation: The rates are 50% and 40%; denominators matter.
choices: Counts alone prove campus B has the higher rate.

questions.stem: A recorded value has z=-1.5. What does that mean?
questions.explanation: A z-score measures signed distance in SD units.
choices: It is 1.5 original units below zero.
It is 1.5 SD below the mean.
It is above 98.5% of values automatically.

questions.stem: A spinner has three colors occupying half, one quarter, and one quarter of its area. Why is assigning each color probability 1/3 inappropriate?
questions.explanation: Equally likely colors require equal chance, not merely three category names.
choices: A spinner cannot have three outcomes.

questions.stem: What equation describes a continuous model's 90th percentile k?
questions.explanation: The percentile cutoff has the stated area to its left.

questions.stem: In 2, 3, 3, 4, 18, the 18 is replaced by 180. What happens?
questions.explanation: The middle position stays the same while the total increases greatly.
choices: The mean increases; the median stays 3.
The median increases more than the mean.

questions.stem: A population proportion interval is 0.30 to 0.42. How should a proposed proportion 0.50 be described?
questions.explanation: Being outside this interval is evidence against compatibility, not an absolute impossibility statement.
choices: Outside the interval and incompatible with this interval estimate.
Compatible because 0.50 is a valid probability.
Proved impossible under every future sample.

figure.alt: A proportion interval 0.30 to 0.42 with proposed value 0.50 to its right.

data.alt: A proportion interval 0.30 to 0.42 with proposed value 0.50 to its right.

questions.stem: A value equals its distribution's mean. What is its z-score?
questions.explanation: Its deviation from the mean is zero.

questions.stem: Ten independent trials each have success probability 0.3. X counts successes. What makes a binomial model appropriate?
questions.explanation: Those experimental conditions define the binomial setting.
choices: The expected count is an integer.
Fixed trial count, two outcomes, independence, and constant success chance.

questions.skill_group: Continuous densities, areas, and cumulative probabilities
questions.stem: F(3)=0.20 and F(7)=0.80 for a continuous variable. What is P(3<X<7)?
questions.explanation: Subtract the cumulative areas at the two cutoffs.

questions.stem: A dot plot has five dots at 2 visits and one dot at 8 visits. What does the stack at 2 mean?
questions.explanation: Each dot represents an observation; a stack records repeated values.

figure.alt: Five dots at 2 visits and one dot at 8 visits.

data.alt: Five dots at 2 visits and one dot at 8 visits.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: For independent observations with finite variance, compare repeated means at n=1 and n=100. What is generally expected?
questions.explanation: Averaging reduces spread, and CLT behavior can change the sampling-distribution shape.
choices: The n=1 histogram must be normal.
Means at n=100 are less spread and often more nearly normal.
The population itself becomes less spread.

questions.stem: A sample has variance 16 seconds squared. What is its standard deviation?
questions.explanation: The standard deviation is the square root of 16 and is measured in seconds.

questions.stem: The ordered data are 2, 4, 4, 7, 20. What is the median?
questions.explanation: The middle observation is the third value, 4.

questions.stem: A one-sample t interval uses n=16. What degrees of freedom are used?
questions.explanation: A one-sample mean t method uses n-1 degrees of freedom.

questions.stem: P(A)=0.4, P(B)=0.5, and their overlap is 0.2. What is P(A OR B)?
questions.explanation: Add the two probabilities and subtract the overlap.

questions.stem: Notebook colors are blue, blue, black, red. Which statement meaningfully summarizes a typical category?
questions.explanation: A most-common category is meaningful without arbitrary arithmetic on labels.
choices: The standard deviation of color names is 1.
Blue is the most common color.

questions.stem: The SD of a normal model increases while the mean stays fixed. What happens to its peak?
questions.explanation: Spreading the same area over a wider curve lowers its peak.
choices: It becomes lower as the curve spreads out.

questions.stem: A student treats z=2 as a probability of 2. What is wrong?
questions.explanation: Z-scores can exceed 1, while probabilities cannot.
choices: A standardized distance is not an area probability.
A z-score must be a percentage.
A normal model cannot have positive z-scores.

questions.stem: For a normal approximation to the probability of at most a given count, which intervals belong in the shaded area?
questions.explanation: At most includes the cutoff count and smaller counts.
choices: The cutoff count's interval and all intervals below it.
Only the intervals above the cutoff count's interval.
Only the intervals below the cutoff count's interval.

questions.stem: Plan A samples students from every building. Plan B randomly chooses two buildings and surveys everyone there. What distinguishes Plan B?
questions.explanation: The second plan selects whole groups, rather than sampling within every group.
choices: It selects some students from every group.
It studies all students in selected groups.
It guarantees all possible student samples are equally likely.

questions.stem: The wait until the next request is modeled as exponential with rate 4 per hour. What is its mean in minutes?
questions.explanation: Mean wait is one quarter hour, or 15 minutes.

questions.stem: X counts broken cables in independent checks. Can broken be called success in a binomial model?
questions.explanation: Success is a modeling label, not a value judgment.
choices: Only if no cables are broken.
Yes; success means the counted outcome.
Only if more than half are broken.

questions.stem: A supplied positive critical z leaves 0.025 to its right. What cumulative area lies to its left?
questions.explanation: Left and right areas total 1.

questions.stem: A value equals its distribution's mean. What is its z-score?
questions.explanation: Its deviation from the mean is zero.

questions.stem: Randomly assigned groups have slightly different initial mean scores. What follows?
questions.explanation: Random assignment balances influences in expectation, not perfectly in each experiment.
choices: The study must have used a census.
Chance imbalance can occur despite random assignment.
Random assignment requires exact matching of every score.

questions.stem: A one-sample t interval uses n=16. What degrees of freedom are used?
questions.explanation: A one-sample mean t method uses n-1 degrees of freedom.

questions.stem: Four cables are sampled uniformly without replacement from 12, of which 5 are faulty. Which model directly fits the faulty count?
questions.explanation: The finite population and no-replacement design fit the hypergeometric model.

questions.stem: An exponential model has mean wait 4 minutes. What is its SD?
questions.explanation: For an exponential distribution, mean and SD are both the reciprocal of the rate.

questions.stem: SE is 4 at n=25. What is SE at n=100, with the same population SD and independence?
questions.explanation: Quadrupling n halves SE.

questions.stem: Score A is 10 above its mean with SD 5; score B is 12 above its mean with SD 12. Which is relatively farther above its group mean?
questions.explanation: A is 2 SD above its mean; B is 1 SD above.
choices: The larger raw score difference always wins.

questions.stem: An independent fair coin has just produced five tails. What is the chance of heads next?
questions.explanation: Past independent outcomes do not change the next toss probability.
choices: Less than 1/2 because tails is favored.
Greater than 1/2 because heads is due.

questions.stem: In 2, 3, 3, 4, 18, the 18 is replaced by 180. What happens?
questions.explanation: The middle position stays the same while the total increases greatly.
choices: The median increases more than the mean.
The mean increases; the median stays 3.

questions.stem: A game's expected prize is 4 dollars. Which entry fee makes expected net gain zero?
questions.explanation: Expected net gain is expected prize minus the fixed fee.
choices: The maximum possible prize regardless of its probability.

questions.stem: Compare one exponential duration with the average of many independent durations. What remains the same?
questions.explanation: Averaging preserves the expected center while reducing variability.
choices: The maximum possible duration becomes finite for the average.

questions.stem: Four cables are sampled uniformly without replacement from 12, of which 5 are faulty. Which model directly fits the faulty count?
questions.explanation: The finite population and no-replacement design fit the hypergeometric model.

questions.stem: A systematic sample starts at ID 3 and takes every tenth ID. Which IDs appear first?
questions.explanation: Add ten to the starting ID at each selection.

questions.stem: 40 of 100 sampled jobs succeed. What is the sample success proportion?
questions.explanation: Divide the success count by the sample size.

questions.stem: For 2, 3, 3, 4, 18, how does the mean compare with the median?
questions.explanation: The high value pulls the mean above the median of 3.
choices: No comparison is possible without a calculator.

questions.stem: All items in a batch tend to be heavy or light together. What is questionable about sqrt(n) times individual SD for the total?
questions.explanation: Positive dependence can make total variation larger than the independent formula predicts.

questions.stem: Tokens are replaced and mixed after each draw. Compared with leaving them out, what does replacement preserve?
questions.explanation: Replacement restores the composition before the next randomized draw.
choices: A decreasing total number of tokens.
The same token being selected every time.
The original color probabilities on each independent draw.

questions.stem: P(Z>1.2)=0.1151. By symmetry, what is P(Z<-1.2)?
questions.explanation: Opposite equal-distance tails have equal positive probability.

questions.stem: A sample-size formula returns 62.2 observations. Which planned integer size meets that minimum?
questions.explanation: Round a required minimum up to avoid falling short.

questions.stem: A U(0,12) wait has already lasted 11 minutes. What is the largest possible additional wait under this model?
questions.explanation: The total wait cannot exceed the upper support endpoint 12.

questions.stem: Two binomial settings have the same fixed number of trials. One has a greater chance of success on each trial. What changes?
questions.explanation: A higher chance of success raises the average count while the trial count still bounds the result.
choices: Both settings have the same expected number of successes.
Every run in that setting yields more successes.
The maximum possible number of successes is greater in that setting.
The expected number of successes is greater in that setting.

questions.stem: A file is 60 KB; its group has mean 50 KB and SD 5 KB. How far above the mean is it?
questions.explanation: The difference is 10 KB, or twice the 5 KB standard deviation.

questions.stem: A strongly skewed variable is converted to z-scores. Does it become normal?
questions.explanation: A linear transformation preserves distributional shape.
choices: Yes; subtracting the mean removes the tail.
Yes; every z-score distribution is standard normal.
No; standardization shifts and rescales without removing skew.

questions.stem: A report gives sample SD=6 minutes and SE=1 minute. Which describes variation among individual observed times?
questions.explanation: Sample SD describes observed individual spread; SE describes mean-estimation precision.

questions.stem: Why report a confidence interval instead of only a sample mean?
questions.explanation: An interval communicates estimation precision beyond a single point estimate.
choices: It guarantees the true mean is the midpoint.
It expresses uncertainty in estimating the population mean.

questions.stem: Students rate a service while its manager watches. Compared with anonymous responses, what might happen?
questions.explanation: Pressure or perceived consequences can influence responses.

questions.stem: A game charges a fixed entry fee and sometimes awards a prize. What distinguishes net gain from the prize amount?
questions.explanation: A player pays the fee whether or not a prize is awarded.
choices: Net gain accounts for the fee paid to play.
Net gain ignores outcomes with no prize.
The fee changes the chance of each prize.
Net gain equals the largest possible prize.

questions.stem: For independent items, the SD of a sum is sqrt(n) times individual SD. Why is n times SD generally wrong?
questions.explanation: Adding variances gives n times variance, hence sqrt(n) times SD.
choices: All individual deviations have the same sign.
Independent variances add; SD is then a square root.

questions.stem: At a tree node, two exhaustive outgoing branch probabilities are 0.6 and 0.5. What is wrong?
questions.explanation: Exhaustive alternative branches at a node must sum to 1.

figure.alt: A proposed tree node has two exhaustive outgoing branches labeled 0.6 and 0.5.

data.alt: A proposed tree node has two exhaustive outgoing branches labeled 0.6 and 0.5.

questions.stem: Two servers share one power supply. Why might independent failure events be a poor model?
questions.explanation: A shared influence can create dependence.
choices: A power failure can affect both servers together.

questions.stem: P(Z>1.2)=0.1151. By symmetry, what is P(Z<-1.2)?
questions.explanation: Opposite equal-distance tails have equal positive probability.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: The CLT supports an approximately normal distribution of large-sample means. What does it not claim?
questions.explanation: The CLT concerns the average or sum, not a transformation of population shape.
choices: Means can have approximately normal sampling distributions.
Larger independent samples can have smaller SE.

questions.stem: A sample has variance 16 seconds squared. What is its standard deviation?
questions.explanation: The standard deviation is the square root of 16 and is measured in seconds.

questions.stem: A selected student's name is removed before the next random draw. What changes?
questions.explanation: Sampling without replacement prevents repeats of the selected individual.
choices: That student cannot be selected again.
Every remaining student becomes impossible to select.
The same name must be selected next.

questions.stem: A proposed normal model gives substantial probability to negative durations. What is the concern?
questions.explanation: A normal approximation may be poor when impossible values receive meaningful probability.
choices: Normal distributions cannot model any positive variable.
It assigns appreciable probability to impossible values.

questions.stem: A researcher stops after a fixed number of draws and counts marked tokens. Which detail best distinguishes the binomial and hypergeometric settings?
questions.explanation: The two models use different sampling designs even though both count successes in a fixed number of draws.
choices: Whether a fixed number of draws is used.
Whether the recorded result is a whole number.
Whether each token is returned and the pool remixed before the next draw.
Whether marked is a desirable outcome.

questions.stem: The slides recommend plus-four when confidence is at least 90% and n>=10. Does n=24 at 85% confidence meet that recommendation?
questions.explanation: Both stated recommendations must be met; this is distinct from the ordinary interval count check.
choices: Yes; plus-four has no stated conditions.
No; the confidence level is below the stated threshold.

questions.stem: A recorded file size is far above the rest. What should happen before deleting it?
questions.explanation: An unusual value can be valid and informative; deletion needs a defensible reason.
choices: Delete it because all outliers are mistakes.
Keep it only if the mean equals the median.
Check whether it is an error or a genuine unusual file.

questions.stem: An exponential waiting time has mean 5 minutes. What rate per minute matches it?
questions.explanation: Rate is the reciprocal of mean wait in consistent units.

source.slide_title: Converting a mean to a rate

questions.stem: Independent sample size increases. What happens to spread in original units?
questions.explanation: Totals aggregate variation while averages divide the total by n.
choices: SD of sums rises; SE of averages falls.

questions.stem: A is 6 above its mean with SD 3; B is 8 above its mean with SD 8. Which is more extreme above its group center?
questions.explanation: Their z-scores are 2 and 1.
choices: The larger raw difference always determines extremeness.

questions.stem: Which sequence gives the first success on trial 4?
questions.explanation: The first three must fail and the fourth must succeed.

questions.stem: Sample SD is 6 minutes and n=9; sqrt(9)=3. What estimated SE is used?
questions.explanation: Estimated SE is s/sqrt(n) and retains the measurement units.

questions.stem: Which event is the complement of at least one failure in three trials?
questions.explanation: The only way to avoid any failure is to have none.

questions.stem: A bell-shaped distribution of scores has mean 50 and standard deviation 5. Approximately what percentage of scores lies between 45 and 55?
questions.explanation: The interval extends one standard deviation on either side of the mean, so the empirical rule gives about 68%.

questions.stem: A cumulative table gives 30% below 5 seconds and 75% below 10 seconds. What percent is from 5 to less than 10?
questions.explanation: Subtract cumulative percentages at the two boundaries.

questions.stem: A U(0,12) wait has already lasted 11 minutes. What is the largest possible additional wait under this model?
questions.explanation: The total wait cannot exceed the upper support endpoint 12.

questions.stem: For a standard normal variable, compare P(Z<-1.4) and P(Z>1.4).
questions.explanation: Normal symmetry makes opposite equal-distance tails equal.

questions.stem: A basic box plot reports minimum 0, Q1=2, median 3, Q3=4, maximum 20. Which comparison is supported?
questions.explanation: Using the displayed summary, the upper segment spans 20-4=16 units and the lower segment spans 2-0=2 units. Segment length describes numerical spread, not an exact observation count; quartile conventions and ties can affect those counts.
choices: The plot establishes the exact mean.
The segment from Q3 to the maximum spans a wider numerical range than the segment from the minimum to Q1.
The upper segment must contain three times as many observations.
The lower segment contains no observations.

figure.alt: Basic box plot: minimum 0, Q1 2, median 3, Q3 4, maximum 20. Whiskers show min and max.

data.alt: Basic box plot: minimum 0, Q1 2, median 3, Q3 4, maximum 20. Whiskers show min and max.

questions.stem: 40 of 100 sampled jobs succeed. What is the sample success proportion?
questions.explanation: Divide the success count by the sample size.

questions.stem: A question asks for the mass exceeded by only 10% of packages. What units should the answer have?
questions.explanation: The requested answer is an original-scale cutoff, not a probability.
choices: No units because it is a z-score automatically.

questions.stem: A game charges a fixed entry fee and sometimes awards a prize. What distinguishes net gain from the prize amount?
questions.explanation: A player pays the fee whether or not a prize is awarded.
choices: The fee changes the chance of each prize.
Net gain ignores outcomes with no prize.
Net gain accounts for the fee paid to play.
Net gain equals the largest possible prize.

questions.stem: A well-run randomized experiment finds better results for an app among its volunteers. Which claim needs extra caution?
questions.explanation: Generalization depends on the volunteers and setting, beyond random assignment.
choices: The observed volunteers had different average results.
The same effect applies to all students everywhere.
Random assignment helped compare the formats.
The study provides evidence about an app effect in this setting.

questions.stem: After an 11-minute wait, U(0,12) allows at most 1 more minute. An exponential model allows longer additional waits. What explains the difference?
questions.explanation: Their supports and conditional-wait behavior differ.
choices: Exponential waits stop at their mean.
Uniform waits have a finite endpoint; exponential waits do not.

questions.stem: To estimate a population mean with unknown population SD using a sample SD, which standard method fits?
questions.explanation: The t method accounts for estimating population SD when constructing an interval for the mean.
choices: A known-SD z interval treating s as known population SD.
A proportion interval regardless of variable type.
A prediction interval for a single future observation.

questions.stem: A model allows counts 0,1,2,... without a finite upper limit. Can it still be discrete?
questions.explanation: Discrete support can be infinite without forming a continuum.
choices: No; a count must stop at 10.
Yes; countably many separated values can be discrete.
Only if every count has equal probability.
No; all infinite possibilities are continuous.

questions.stem: Datasets share min=0 and max=100, but have different IQRs. What follows?
questions.explanation: Range uses endpoints while IQR uses quartile positions.
choices: Equal ranges do not imply equal middle-half spread.
Their standard deviations must be identical.

questions.stem: A supplied sampling model gives P(mean<=12)=0.90. What is P(mean>12)?
questions.explanation: The two events are complements.

questions.stem: The mean waiting count is 4 trials. Must the first success occur by trial 4?
questions.explanation: A geometric distribution has no finite maximum waiting count.
choices: Yes; the mean is a deadline.
No; it must occur exactly on trial 5.

questions.stem: A first branch has probability 0.4; its next conditional branch is 0.5. What is the path probability?
questions.explanation: Multiply probabilities along a path.

questions.stem: X counts trials through first success. What does X>3 require?
questions.explanation: Waiting more than three trials means no success in those trials.
choices: Failures on the first three trials.
At least one success in the first three trials.

questions.stem: Ratings poor, fair, good, excellent are coded 1 through 4. What is safest to infer from the codes?
questions.explanation: Ordered categories establish rank, not equal measurement distances.
choices: Excellent is exactly twice as favorable as fair.
Each adjacent rating differs by exactly one unit of satisfaction.
Excellent ranks above good, but equal numerical gaps are not established.

questions.stem: A fixed 5-kg container is added to a shipment of random item masses. What changes?
questions.explanation: A fixed additive quantity shifts the distribution without adding random variability.
choices: Both mean and SD rise by 5 kg.
Expected total rises by 5 kg; total SD is unchanged.

questions.stem: A dataset has mean 8. One observation below 8 is removed. What happens to the mean of the remaining values?
questions.explanation: Removing a below-average observation raises the remaining average.

questions.stem: For a normal model, where is the 10th percentile?
questions.explanation: The lowest tenth ends on the lower side of the symmetric center.

questions.stem: A normal model has mean 50 and SD 2. Which interval contains about 99.7%?
questions.explanation: The empirical rule uses three SD on each side.

questions.stem: For an exponential wait, which one-minute interval has more probability?
questions.explanation: An exponential density decreases with waiting time.

figure.alt: A declining exponential density highlights 0 to 1 minute and 5 to 6 minutes.

data.alt: A declining exponential density highlights 0 to 1 minute and 5 to 6 minutes.

questions.stem: A one-sample t interval uses n=16. What degrees of freedom are used?
questions.explanation: A one-sample mean t method uses n-1 degrees of freedom.

questions.stem: A file is 60 KB; its group has mean 50 KB and SD 5 KB. How far above the mean is it?
questions.explanation: The difference is 10 KB, or twice the 5 KB standard deviation.

questions.stem: A box plot has median 6. Can it reveal exactly how many observations equal 5?
questions.explanation: A box plot compresses the data into a few summary positions.
choices: No; the summary does not retain those exact counts.

questions.stem: The slides recommend plus-four when confidence is at least 90% and n>=10. Does n=24 at 85% confidence meet that recommendation?
questions.explanation: Both stated recommendations must be met; this is distinct from the ordinary interval count check.
choices: Yes; plus-four has no stated conditions.
No; the confidence level is below the stated threshold.

questions.stem: On a die, A is even and B is greater than 3. Which results satisfy both?
questions.explanation: The intersection contains results meeting both conditions.

questions.stem: The success chance improves after each failed attempt because the process learns. Why is a geometric model questionable?
questions.explanation: Geometric waiting assumes independent trials with a constant success chance.
choices: The success probability is not constant.

questions.stem: Three reported percentages are 33.3%, 33.3%, and 33.3%. What most reasonably explains the 99.9% total?
questions.explanation: Rounding can make displayed percentages differ slightly from 100%.

questions.stem: To halve SE, how must an independent sample's size change?
questions.explanation: Squaring the desired precision factor gives the sample-size factor.
choices: Add 4 regardless of its current size.

questions.stem: A nonnormal variable has a well-defined mean and SD. Can its z-score automatically be looked up as a standard-normal probability?
questions.explanation: Standardization is broadly possible, but normal probabilities require a normal model.
choices: No; only normal variables can be standardized.
Yes; a positive SD is sufficient.
No; the normal shape assumption still matters.

questions.stem: Which t distribution has heavier tails?
questions.explanation: Small degrees of freedom produce heavier tails and greater critical values.

questions.stem: Four cables are sampled uniformly without replacement from 12, of which 5 are faulty. Which model directly fits the faulty count?
questions.explanation: The finite population and no-replacement design fit the hypergeometric model.

questions.stem: For an exponential wait, which one-minute interval has more probability?
questions.explanation: An exponential density decreases with waiting time.

figure.alt: A declining exponential density highlights 0 to 1 minute and 5 to 6 minutes.

data.alt: A declining exponential density highlights 0 to 1 minute and 5 to 6 minutes.

questions.stem: Which shortcut finds at least one success in a fixed set of independent trials?
questions.explanation: At least one success is the complement of zero successes.
choices: The probability of exactly one success only.
1 minus the probability of no successes.

questions.stem: A wait is uniform from 0 to 12 minutes. What is P(3<X<6)?
questions.explanation: The interval occupies 3 of the support's 12 minutes.

questions.stem: A model describes the mass of one package. Is its SD automatically appropriate for the mean mass of 100 independent packages?
questions.explanation: Units can match while distributions and spreads differ.
choices: Yes; both are measured in grams.
No; the average has less spread.

questions.stem: Notebook colors are blue, blue, black, red. Which statement meaningfully summarizes a typical category?
questions.explanation: A most-common category is meaningful without arbitrary arithmetic on labels.
choices: Blue is the most common color.
The standard deviation of color names is 1.

questions.stem: Independent trials have a constant chance of success strictly between zero and one. Which variable can take arbitrarily large values?
questions.explanation: There can be any number of failures before a first success.
choices: The number of trials through the first success.
The number of successes in a fixed set of trials.
The number of outcomes on one yes-or-no trial.
The number of marked items in a fixed-size sample.

questions.stem: A fair coin gives 8 heads in 10 tosses. What follows?
questions.explanation: Long-run probability does not impose exact counts in short sequences.
choices: The next two tosses must be tails.
Such a short-run imbalance can occur with a fair coin.
The coin's future head probability is now 0.8.
Fairness requires exactly 5 heads in every ten tosses.

questions.stem: A mean interval is 10 to 14 minutes. Which report matches its target?
questions.explanation: The reported target is the population mean, with confidence understood as procedure coverage.
choices: Every future duration will be between 10 and 14.
The procedure estimates the population mean duration between 10 and 14 minutes.
The median is guaranteed to equal 12.
Exactly 95 of the next 100 durations will lie there.

questions.stem: Frequencies for 0, 1, 2, and 3 jobs are 2, 3, 4, and 1. How many sessions had at most 1 job?
questions.explanation: At most 1 includes the frequencies for both 0 and 1.

questions.stem: Twenty items have sample mean mass 5 g. What is their total mass?
questions.explanation: Sample sum equals n times sample mean.

questions.stem: 400 people are sampled without replacement from 20,000. Does this meet the at-most-10% sample-fraction guideline?
questions.explanation: 400/20,000=0.02, within the stated guideline.
choices: Yes; any random sample meets it.

questions.stem: Why represent a single binomial count by an interval when using a normal approximation?
questions.explanation: The interval lets continuous area approximate the discrete probability mass.
choices: The count can take fractional values.
An interval has area under a continuous curve, while a single point has zero area.
A count always equals its expected value.
The normal distribution has positive probability at every exact point.

questions.stem: To estimate a population mean with unknown population SD using a sample SD, which standard method fits?
questions.explanation: The t method accounts for estimating population SD when constructing an interval for the mean.
choices: A prediction interval for a single future observation.
A proportion interval regardless of variable type.
A known-SD z interval treating s as known population SD.

questions.stem: Box plot A has median 12, IQR 4; B has median 9, IQR 8. Which statement is supported?
questions.explanation: The summaries compare centers and middle spreads, not every pair of observations.
choices: A has higher median and smaller middle-half spread.
B has higher median and smaller spread.
A has lower median and larger spread.
Every value in A exceeds every value in B.

figure.alt: Basic box plots: A has median 12 and IQR 4; B has median 9 and IQR 8. Whiskers show min and max.

data.alt: Basic box plots: A has median 12 and IQR 4; B has median 9 and IQR 8. Whiskers show min and max.

questions.stem: A bar graph of counts 98 and 100 starts its vertical axis at 97. What impression might it exaggerate?
questions.explanation: A truncated baseline can make a small count difference appear visually large.
choices: The size of the difference between the counts.

questions.stem: A mean interval is 10 to 14. How should a proposed mean of 12 be described?
questions.explanation: Every interior value is compatible with the interval; the midpoint is not a certainty.
choices: Compatible with the interval, without being proved exact.
Proved to be the exact population mean.

figure.alt: Interval 10 to 14 and proposed mean 12 marked at the center.

data.alt: Interval 10 to 14 and proposed mean 12 marked at the center.

questions.stem: A proposed normal model gives substantial probability to negative durations. What is the concern?
questions.explanation: A normal approximation may be poor when impossible values receive meaningful probability.
choices: Normal distributions cannot model any positive variable.
It assigns appreciable probability to impossible values.

questions.stem: Plan A checks 10 items and counts successes. Plan B checks until the first success and counts trials. Which is geometric under independent constant-p trials?
questions.explanation: A geometric variable counts trials through the first success.

questions.stem: A buyer counts rejected items among a fixed number of independent inspections with the same rejection chance. What should be called a success for this model?
questions.explanation: The counted category determines what is labeled success.
choices: A rejection, because that is what the variable counts.
An acceptance, because success must be favorable.
A change in the rejection chance.

questions.stem: A service meets its deadline with probability 0.80. What is the probability of missing it?
questions.explanation: The complement has probability 1-0.80.

questions.stem: Uniform model A spans width 4; model B spans width 8. Which density is taller?
questions.explanation: A narrower rectangular support requires a taller density to preserve total area 1.
choices: The one with the larger mean regardless of width.

questions.stem: A uniform interval centered at 10 doubles its width while keeping center 10. What happens?
questions.explanation: Uniform mean depends on midpoint; SD is proportional to width.

questions.stem: A known-SD mean interval currently has margin 1. To target margin 0.5 at the same confidence, how should n change?
questions.explanation: Halving a square-root-based margin requires four times the observations.

questions.stem: A normal model's SD doubles with mean fixed. What happens to its model IQR?
questions.explanation: Normal quartile distances scale with SD.

questions.stem: To estimate a population mean with unknown population SD using a sample SD, which standard method fits?
questions.explanation: The t method accounts for estimating population SD when constructing an interval for the mean.
choices: A known-SD z interval treating s as known population SD.
A prediction interval for a single future observation.
A proportion interval regardless of variable type.

questions.stem: A model has one blank probability entry and lists every possible value. What does the blank need to account for?
questions.explanation: The outcomes in the completed table must account for the entire probability mass.
choices: Half the total probability, regardless of the other entries.
The average of the listed probabilities.
All probability not already assigned to the other values.
The probability of the most likely listed value.

questions.stem: A mean is estimated from grouped intervals using midpoints. Why is it generally approximate?
questions.explanation: Grouping hides exact values, so midpoint weighting replaces them with approximations.
choices: The sample size is necessarily unknown.
Frequencies cannot be used in means.
Actual observations need not equal the interval midpoints.

questions.stem: A small prize is common and a large prize is rare. Why is the midpoint between the prizes generally a poor estimate of the expected payout?
questions.explanation: Expected value weights each outcome by its probability.
choices: The small prize does not count toward the average.
The expected payout must equal the larger prize.
It gives the two prizes equal weight despite their different chances.
Only the larger prize determines the mean.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: Someone says n=30 guarantees normal sample means for every population. What is the problem?
questions.explanation: There is no universal cutoff guaranteeing a good normal approximation.
choices: Thirty is too large for any sample.
Only populations with mean zero qualify.
Sample means can never approach normality.
Skewness and extreme observations affect how large n needs to be.

questions.stem: A grouped table reports 12 durations from 5 to less than 10 seconds. Can it tell exactly how many equal 7 seconds?
questions.explanation: Grouping preserves interval counts but loses individual values.
choices: No; exact positions within the interval are hidden.

questions.stem: Which sequence gives the first success on trial 4?
questions.explanation: The first three must fail and the fourth must succeed.
